Here's a Jimi Hendrix fact that stopped us cold.  In July 1967—right in the middle of his rise to global fame—Hendrix quietly walked into a studio to record with his old friend Curtis Knight. Not for a record deal. Not for money. He picked up a guitar and a Hagstrom 8-string bass (an instrument he'd barely touched before) just to honor their friendship and help settle an old contract dispute.  No one made him do it. He just showed up.  That loyalty, that generosity—it's part of what made Hendrix one of a kind. And it's part of what Kiss The Sky: RE-Experience Hendrix Tribute honors every single night they take the stage. Here's a Billy Joel fact that genuinely surprises most people.  Before 'Piano Man,' before Madison Square Garden, before any of it—a 21-year-old Billy Joel spent 1970 in a two-man proto-metal band called Attila. His instrument? A Hammond B-3 organ run through wah-wah pedals and a Marshall stack. The album cover had the duo dressed as ancient Huns. It was loud, unconventional, and completely unlike anything we associate with him now.  It only lasted one album. Then Joel went in an entirely different direction—and the rest is the catalog we all know by heart.  Full story here: https://ultimateclassicrock.com/billy-joel-attila/  Kyle Martin's Piano Man brings that full Billy Joel legacy to the stage—from the deep cuts to the anthems. Did you know Priscilla Presley's memoir accidentally inspired one of Depeche Mode's biggest hits?  In 1985, Priscilla published Elvis and Me—her firsthand account of life with Elvis, their relationship, and what it meant to have someone be your guide, your protector, your entire world. Martin Gore read it, and the idea behind 'Personal Jesus' came directly from those pages. The song is about being a Jesus for someone else—giving them hope, being their anchor. He found that story in Priscilla's words.  She didn't know until much later.  That's the kind of legacy that travels. From Graceland to synth-pop radio—Priscilla's story has shaped more of music history than most people realize. Here's something most Billy Joel fans don't know.  When he recorded 'The Longest Time,' he wanted that full 1950s doo-wop group sound—tight harmonies, four voices blending together. But instead of hiring singers, he did something remarkable: he sang every single vocal part himself, then spliced all the tracks together.  What you hear on the recording? That's one man pretending to be a quartet. And pulling it off completely.  It's that kind of dedication to the craft that makes Kyle Martin's Piano Man such a special show. Kyle brings that same attention to Billy Joel's music every time he takes the stage—the arrangements, the energy, the songs you grew up with performed the way they deserve to be. Here's a studio story that still gives us chills.  During the recording of 'Song for Guy,' engineer Stuart Epps noticed mid-take that the tape reel was nearly gone—just feet remaining—with Elton still deep in the performance. Nobody stopped him. Nobody could. The last chord rang out, and the tape ran dry right at that final moment. One more mistake, one longer outro, and that song disappears forever.  It's one of those behind-the-scenes moments that makes you hear a piece of music completely differently.  The Rocket Man Show has spent years honoring exactly this kind of legacy—the songs that almost weren't, played the way they were always meant to be heard. Live, full, and without a safety net.  Which Elton John song would you be most heartbroken to lose? Drop it in the comments—we want to know.
